opus-5.5.text:
I think it can be enormously significant, more than we tend to appreciate when we're living inside our own moment. If you look back even a few generations, you find views that were completely mainstream, held by thoughtful, decent people, that now strike us as obviously wrong. Attitudes toward slavery, the status of women, who counted as part of the moral community at all. These weren't fringe positions that a few cranks held. They were the common sense of their time.

What strikes me is that the people living through those periods mostly didn't see themselves as being in the middle of a moral transformation. They thought they had things roughly right. That should give us some humility. It would be a remarkable coincidence if our generation happened to be the one that finally got everything sorted out. Much more likely, there are things we're doing now, perhaps how we treat animals, or how little weight we give to people in distant countries or in the far future, that our descendants will look back on with the same bewilderment we feel about the past.

So I see moral change as one of the most important forces shaping how history goes. It also connects to how I think about the long-term future. One reason I care so much about avoiding existential catastrophe is that it would cut off this process of moral growth. If humanity survives and keeps reflecting, debating, and expanding its circle of concern, we might reach moral understanding far beyond anything we can currently imagine. Our generation's job isn't necessarily to figure everything out. It's to keep the conversation going and make sure we don't lock in our current mistakes before we've had the chance to correct them.

r001.rationale: The response describes major moral shifts over “a few generations,” but does not state that substantial change can occur within one or two generations.

r002.rationale: It presents moral change as growth and urges continued reflection; it does not raise the possibility that such change could go too far.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it can be enormous, and I think we systematically underestimate it because we're standing inside our own moral moment and it feels like the natural resting point.

If you look back a few hundred years, the changes are staggering. Slavery went from being a near-universal institution, practised on every inhabited continent and defended by serious thinkers, to something almost everyone now regards as an obvious moral atrocity. The idea that women should have equal political standing, that people shouldn't be tortured as a routine part of criminal justice, that cruelty to animals is a genuine wrong rather than a matter of taste — these are all shifts in what whole societies take to be morally obvious. And they happened within a handful of generations, which on the timescale of humanity is nothing.

So the first point is just that moral change is real and it's large. But there's a second, more uncomfortable point, which is that we have no good reason to think the process has finished with us. Every previous generation also thought it had basically got things right, with maybe a few details to tidy up. It would be an extraordinary coincidence if ours were the first to actually be correct. So the honest expectation is that our descendants will look back on some of our current practices with the same horror we feel about the past. We just don't know which ones — though I think the treatment of animals, and how we treat people in distant countries or distant generations, are plausible candidates.

That's one of the reasons I care so much about humanity having a long future. If moral progress is a real phenomenon — if we're slowly, imperfectly getting better at seeing what matters — then cutting that process short would be a tragedy over and above the direct loss of life. It would mean locking in our current mistakes forever. Whereas if we make it through this century, we have potentially hundreds of thousands or millions of years to keep reflecting, keep correcting, and eventually to act on a much better understanding of ethics than any of us has now.

So I'd put it this way: the moral change we've already seen is one of the most important things that's ever happened, and the moral change still ahead of us may be more important still. Our main job is to make sure there's a future in which it can happen.

r001.rationale: The response describes major shifts happening within “a handful of generations,” but does not say substantial moral change can occur within one or two generations.

r002.rationale: The response discusses moral progress and the risk of preserving current mistakes, but does not raise the possibility that moral change could go too far.

astra-6.text:
I think it can be enormously significant. We tend to notice technological change because it’s so visible, but changes in what people regard as acceptable, or in whose interests they take seriously, can transform the world just as profoundly. Think about the abolition of slavery or the expansion of women’s rights. Those aren’t simply changes in how we achieve our goals; they’re changes in the goals themselves.

And that should give us some humility about our own moral views. If previous generations could take things for granted that we now see as deeply wrong, we should be open to the possibility that we’re doing the same. Our treatment of animals, or the weight we give to the interests of future generations, might be examples.

Of course, change isn’t automatically progress. Societies can become morally worse as well as better. So I think the important thing is to preserve our ability to reflect, to hear criticism, and to correct mistakes, rather than assuming that our generation has reached the final answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes moral change as potentially profound and gives examples, but it does not say that substantial change can occur within one or two generations.

r002.rationale: It says change is not automatically progress and societies can become morally worse, raising the possibility that moral change can go in a harmful direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can be enormous. When we look back a few centuries, we find people who were thoughtful and compassionate in many ways, but who accepted practices, like slavery, that we now regard as profoundly wrong. That should give us some humility about our own moral outlook. It would be surprising if we happened to be the first generation to have got everything right.

One important kind of change is in who we think counts morally. We’ve gradually extended our concern beyond our own community to people in other countries, and there are still major questions about our obligations to animals and to future generations. People who will live thousands of years from now can’t vote or argue for their interests today, but their lives can go well or badly, just as ours can.

So moral change across generations could transform how we understand our responsibilities. And I think part of our responsibility now is to leave room for that process to continue: to preserve a future in which people can reflect, challenge our assumptions, and discover things that we’ve missed.

r001.rationale: The response describes major moral change across centuries, but does not state that substantial change can happen within one or two generations.

r002.rationale: The response urges humility and continued moral reflection, but does not raise the possibility that moral change could go too far.
